speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the rumours we are hearing are true, the Thirty-third Parliament will be dissolved in a matter of days. Twenty-seven women out of a total of 282 Members were elected to the House of Commons.
I rise today to pay tribute to three of my colleagues who will be leaving this House shortly. 1 speak of Madam Therese Killens, the Hon. Pat Carney, and Miss Pauline Jewett. All three have played a very important role in leading the women of this country into public life. Their insight and intelligence have helped in the formulation of policy and legislation, and the fair and lucid critique of legislation once formulated. [Translation]
Therese Killens was dedicated to the cause of the disabled and the homeless. She did not make a lot of noise, but we remember her for her effectiveness and for what she accomplished in the area of pensions for women working in the home. [English]
Pauline Jewett will be remembered for her work in both judicial committees and constitutional committees. At a time when women managed to mobilize their forces to entrench the basic right to equality in the Constitution, it was noteworthy that women such as Pauline Jewett provided courage, strength, and inspiration.
Pat Carney, who was at the forefront of one of the most important debates facing the country, should also be lauded for her ability to hold her own and be fair, for her ability to voice her opinion and to be heard, as well as for her ability to listen.
To all of these women I wish good luck in their future endeavours. As a recent arrival in politics, 1 also extend my many thanks.

Mr. Speaker, the protection of its citizens is a valued right in any country. In this regard concern is being expressed by Canadians and an international human rights organization about the plight of a Canadian citizen, a resident of Etobicoke North. I refer to Balkar Singh in detention in India since November 2, 1987.
The renowned international organization, Amnesty International, in a report last month urged the Indian Government to release him or charge him, and bring him to trial under normal judicial procedures, with all customary legal safeguards.
While recognizing the efforts of the Government to obtain consular access to the detainee to ensure adequate medical treatment and cessation of torture, I would like Members to join with me in urging the Indian Government to bring Balkar Singh to trial at the earliest opportunity, and urge the Government of Canada to continue in its worthy efforts to bring the matter to an early resolve.

Mr. Speaker, Canada has lost one of its best patriots and best philosophers in the death of George Grant.
The man who wrote Lament for a Nation in 1965, lamenting the capitulation of Canadian identity and values to American pressure, is now to be lamented for himself by many Canadians who saw and heard in George Grant and his writings someone who understood what Canada had been about, and what we could be if we resist rather than give in to the temptation of continentalism, the American technological ethos, and the poverty of spirit that lies at the root of advanced liberal capitalism.
George Grant was one who understood the modern mind, who could discern and explore the moral fault lines and crevices of what the modern mind takes for granted as objective reality, but which is really no more than a collectively held uncritical belief.

September 28, 1988
In his books, Technology and Empire, English-Speaking Justice and Technology and Justice, he has given us a warning, too often unheeded, about the new tyranny that we court by turning our backs on the best of our philosophical and political traditions.
If the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement goes through, George Grant will have been spared from the final assault on the Canada he loved. If it does not, perhaps there is yet time to recover and play reveille for a country saved and a philosopher vindicated.

Mr. Speaker, the Royal Canadian Mint enjoys a proud reputation as one of the foremost producers of high quality precious metal coins in the entire world. Maple Leaf gold coins are sought out by coin collectors, investors, and those looking for a secure store of value.
Canada is a major producer of platinum, so it is only natural that we should also get into the platinum coin business.
Last Thursday's special striking ceremony initiating the production of platinum Maple Leaf coins, marks, I am sure, the start of what will be another highly successful venture by the Royal Canadian Mint.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, last June the Federal Court of Canada ruled that the Unemployment Insurance Act was unfair to natural parents because it denied them the benefits for child care enjoyed by adoptive parents.
This decision makes a clear distinction between maternity benefits, which are received by women for health reasons, and parental benefits, which are paid to adoptive parents for the child's care and emotional development.

The Conservative Government has until September 30 to appeal this decision, if it wishes to take such a retrograde step. New Democrats hope that instead the Government will listen to groups such as the Canadian Labour Congress, the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women, and the National Association of Women and the Law, and accept the ruling by implementing parental leave for Canadian parents without jeopardizing maternity leave benefits.
September 28, 1988

This move will finally ensure that Canada provides child care benefits already available in other industrialized countries.

subsubtopic: SALES TAX REFORM-POSITION OF LIBERAL PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, so the Liberals are starting to unveil their election promises and their Leader says that they would not proceed with sales tax reform. They would instead tinker with the present 12 per cent manufacturers' sales tax, perpetuating its unfairness, continuing to disadvantage our domestic manufacturers.
Perhaps the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) should check with the members of his Party who sit on the Finance Committee with me and have shown considerable interest in substantial sales tax reform. But splits on Party policy are not new to the Liberal Party.
Of course, what else could we expect from the Liberal Leader, who, when he was Minister of Finance in the 1970s, was the "Father of the Deficit", raising expenditures nearly 30 per cent per year without increasing revenues, starting the inflationary spiral which led to the recession earlier this decade.
Once again the Liberals have shown that they are the Party of the past, with policies to hurt exporters, to kill jobs. Old ways, old times-Canadians will not be fooled. They want, they demand better.

Mr. Speaker, education ought to be a priority for all Governments. We on this side of the House place a high regard on the educational institutions in our country. We also have an understanding of the financial sacrifices that students must make while studying at a post-secondary institution.
It was with some dismay that I learned that the Government taxes graduate scholarships. Recently I received a letter from a graduate student in Sudbury, Ontario, who had received a $9,000 scholarship for her studies in 1987-88. When she completed her tax return she found that she had to pay $2,000 in taxes. Mr. Speaker, this is unjust. The Government should encourage academic excellence in our youth. This can only benefit the country as a whole. To turn around and tax the
very moneys students are using to upgrade themselves is absolutely ridiculous.
Under this Government we have seen the most substantial tax increases in Canadian history. The problem is that the wrong people are the ones targeted to pay taxes. Why tax a student bursary, and not the 60,000 profitable companies that each year pay no taxes, or the 5,220 taxpayers who made over $50,000 last year and paid no tax, or the 40 people who made over $250,000 last year and paid no tax?
It is time for the Government of Canada to take students into consideration. It is time for the Government to call an election so the people of Canada can have a choice to make in the next election.

Mr. Speaker, 1 too have a question for the Minister responsible for Fitness and Amateur Sport and it concerns the Ben Johnson case. As the Minister knows, there are a lot of unanswered questions which 1 think warrant an immediate investigation.
Yesterday in the House the Minister said that Ben Johnson was tested in Zurich about a month ago, after the competition there, and the tests were negative for steroids. He had been tested some seven other times and all the tests were negative. On the other hand, the IOC said a couple of days ago that there was evidence of long-term steroid use.
There seems to be a contradiction here. I wonder if the Minister can tell the House today why there is a contradiction of that sort. Can he explain the discrepancy of, on the one hand, the IOC saying that there is long-term use of steroids, while on the other hand he has always tested negative?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of State (Youth) and Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)):

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member refers to the results of the tests and the fact that Ben Johnson has been tested approximately, to my best knowledge, eight times in the last 21 months. Furthermore, in
that 21-month period he had been out of training for a four or five-month period because of an injury.
I am not an expert in this area and neither is the Hon. Member, as far as I know, or other Members of this House. I do not know whether there is a contradiction or not. Some of the explanations that I have both read and heard seem to indicate there is no contradiction, in fact, between testing negative at the Zurich meet and testing positive at another point in time. Not being an expert in that area 1 will not seek in any way, shape, or form to replace that expertise.
Suffice it to say that Dr. Dugal, a member of one of the committees of the IOC Medical Commission, a Canadian who was part of the group there who received the test and evaluated it, made some comments today in le Journal de Montreal, and he seems to be very unequivocal about the results of the test and what they mean.

Mr. Speaker, I do remind the Minister that he has at his disposal experts in the field with a lot of training and experience, and that the IOC said that there was evidence of long-term steroid use. Meanwhile, Ben Johnson had been tested negatively eight times in the last 21 months. I wonder if the Minister can explain that discrepancy.
At the same time I wonder if the Minister can explain to the House why, as a matter of policy, Canadian athletes are not tested before they leave the country to go to international meets?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of State (Youth) and Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Youth), Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Minister of State (Youth)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I indicated yesterday that we will have an inquiry and we will take the time to sit down with those who are concerned to make sure that we have some understanding of the terms and where we want to go with this inquiry. I hope that through this process we will offer an opportunity for Ben Johnson to speak and to be heard because Canadians want to hear what he has to say. It is important that he have that opportunity.
In the meantime, may I remind Hon. Members of exactly how the system works. In the case of Mr. Johnson, a test is taken. The IOC makes its determination, and it has made a decision to suspend him for the rest of the Games. That decision is without appeal. Obviously the Games will finish.
The IAAF, the international body for track and field, then enters in and suspends him for a period of two years. The Canadian Track and Field Association follows suit. That is the third instance. Automatically, the rules we have had since 1985-86 provide that the Canadian Government takes notice of that decision and then imposes its sanction.
After that has been done, of course the international federation provides for a 30-day appeal period. That is going on now and an opportunity is provided to the athlete to appeal that decision. If he is successful in his appeal, then the suspension will be withdrawn, as it should be. If he is not successful or if he chooses not to enter into the appeal, then after a period of two years the athlete will have an opportunity to appeal directly to the Canadian Government Minister to have his suspension lifted and then to be reintegrated.
That is the process that we have been following, the process that applies to each and every athlete in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a number of petitions from residents of Delta, Surrey, particularly Crescent Beach, and Tsawwassen, British Columbia.
The petitioners state that when the South Moresby Park Agreement was signed the federal Government committed itself to spending $20 million or more to explore for minerals and hydrocarbons in this First National Marine Park. They point out, however, that exploring for hydrocarbons in these waters is dangerous.
The West Coast of British Columbia is Canada's most earthquake-prone region, and the Queen Charlotte area has an even higher earthquake activity than the San Andreas Fault.
Therefore, the petitioners do not want any more hydrocarbon exploration activities to take place in their coastal waters, be they initiated by the public or private sector, nor do they want government to pay for any such activities.
As in duty bound, the petitioners pray.

Mr. Speaker, I, too, have a petition to present from people in Port Coquitlam, Port Moody, Tsawwassen, and other points along the lower mainland of British Columbia. They are petitioning the House and asking that all exploration activities agreed to in the South Moresby Park Agreement be discontinued and that the Government not pay for any such activities, a commitment of $20 million having been made in the South Moresby Park Agreement.
They also point out that the earthquake danger is higher than the San Andreas Fault in California, that the sea in that area is among the roughest and most unpredictable in the world, and that it could be a potential ecological disaster to open up a hole into an oil well in that area.

Mr. Speaker, I have several different petitions to present, all of them approved according to the rules, Standing Order 106.
One of them is from citizens of several places in Ontario who are very concerned that Bill C-55 threatens Canada's traditional commitment to assisting refugees. They are afraid that most refugees who reach our borders will be turned away without having the merits of their case heard, because there is no sufficient appeal except on points of law, because the safe third country notion has no foundation in law, no definition, and because the standing committee of Parliament produced three years ago a far better, fairer and quicker system for dealing with refugee claims within Canada.
Therefore, they request that Parliament ensure that the Government withdraw Bill C-55, substitute legislation embodying the principles of fair and quick oral hearings of claims of refugee claimants, and that there be universal access to such hearings for every applicant in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I also have a petition from a number of residents of Canada who are concerned that the South Moresby Park Agreement, which was signed in June, means that the federal Government is committing itself to spending $20 million or more to explore for minerals and hydrocarbons in what it is calling the First National Marine Park.
They point out that mining or drilling will render the whole concept of park creation meaningless. They also point out that the West Coast is Canada's most earthquake-prone zone and that the Hecate Strait is among the roughest and most unpredictable seas in the world.
Therefore, they request that Parliament understand that they do not want any more hydrocarbon exploration to take place in the coastal waters, and that they do not want the Government to be paying for it.

Mr. Speaker, I also have petitions from a number of residents of the City of Toronto who are concerned with the promise that the Government made nearly three years ago that Canadian permanent residents should have the same right as Canadian citizens to sponsor parents of any age.
They are asking the Government to have that promise fulfilled now.

Finally, Mr. Speaker, I have a petition from a number of residents of Toronto who point out that the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal threatens the very fabric of Canadian sovereignty, has no mandate from the Canadian people, would reduce Canada's ability to plan the economic, social, and cultural programs that we need, and would integrate Canada further into the North American defence industrial base.
Therefore, the undersigned ask Parliament to ensure that the national debate takes place on the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal and that this debate results in a national general election before any agreement is finalized.

Mr. Speaker, it is also my duty to present to this House a number of petitions coming from residents of southeast New Brunswick, more particularly from the communities of Albert, West

River, Hopewell Cape, Riverside, Pennfield, and many other communities in Albert County.
These petitioners feel that they are not being treated fairly in that the Government has changed the admissibility period for UIC from 10 weeks to 16 weeks. In their case, the Government is not taking any action to change the regulations so that the admissibility period is brought back to 10 weeks, and this action was taken by this Government in other parts of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I have a petition from a number of people in Port Coquitlam, Coquitlam, and in Port Moody, British Columbia, who say that on July 12, 1988, when the South Moresby Park Agreement was signed, the federal Government committed itself to spending $20 million or more to explore for hydrocarbons in the South Moresby marine park.
Whereas the Queen Charlotte region has higher earthquake activity than the San Andreas Fault in California, whereas Hecate Strait has the roughest, most unpredictable sea in the world, the undersigned do not want any more hydrocarbon exploration activities to take place in their coastal waters, nor do they want this Government to pay for such activities.
I may say, having visited all those areas, that I agree with the petitioners and that 1 am proud to present these petitions.
